# Advanced Filters

An advanced filter, also called a document filter, restricts a RAG search to the documents that match a condition, such as a tag, a metadata value, or a date range. Only documents that pass the filter are ranked by semantic similarity, so results never include documents outside the filter. For a task-oriented walkthrough, see [How to filter RAG results by metadata, tags and date](https://aivax.net/blog/filter-rag-results-by-metadata-tags-date/).

Filters are evaluated **before** the search terms are embedded. When no document in the requested collections matches the filter, the request returns an empty result without generating embeddings or charging for the search.

```text
tags has "finance"
metadata.department = "finance" and createdAt >= now-30d
(tags has "finance" or tags has "legal") and not tags has "draft"
```

## Anatomy of a Filter

A filter is one or more **conditions** joined by `and`, `or`, and `not`. Every condition has three parts:

```text
metadata.pages   >   10
└── field ──┘   └op┘ └value┘
```

- **Field** — what to look at: `name`, `content`, `reference`, `tags`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, or `metadata.<key>`. See [Fields](#fields).
- **Operator** — how to compare: `=`, `>`, `contains`, `in`, `has`, `exists`, and others. See [Operators](#operators).
- **Value** — a literal to compare against: a quoted string, a number, `true`, `false`, `null`, a date, or a list in parentheses. See [Values](#values).

The value must always be a literal. Functions, arithmetic, type conversions, and comparisons between two fields are not supported. Keywords, operators, and field names are case-insensitive: `AND`, `And`, and `and` are equivalent.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | text | The document name (`docid` in JSONL imports). |
| `content` | text | The indexed document text. |
| `reference` | text | The document reference that groups related documents, such as chunks of one source. Documents without a reference never match a positive condition on it. |
| `tags` | list of text | The document tags (`__tags`). |
| `createdAt` | date and time | When the document was created. |
| `updatedAt` | date and time | When the document was last updated. |
| `metadata.<key>` | JSON value | A value inside the document metadata (`__meta`). |

See [Documents](documents.md#anatomy-of-a-document) for how these fields are set.

## Operators

Each operator works only with specific fields and value types. Any other combination, such as `tags = "x"` or `name > "a"`, is rejected.

### Equality

| Operator | Meaning | Fields | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `=` | Equals | `name`, `content`, `reference`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `metadata.<key>` | `name = "refund-policy"` |
| `!=` | Not equals; exactly `not field = value` | Same as `=` | `metadata.lang != "en"` |

For `metadata.<key>`, the value may be text, a number, `true`, `false`, or `null`. Text comparison ignores letter case and accents; see [Strings](#strings).

### Ordering

| Operator | Meaning | Fields | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `>` `>=` `<` `<=` | Greater or less than | `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, numeric `metadata.<key>` | `metadata.pages > 10` |

Ordering works on dates for `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, and on **numbers only** for metadata. Dates or text stored in metadata cannot be ordered; see [Metadata](#metadata).

### Text

| Operator | Meaning | Fields | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `contains` | Includes the text; at least 3 characters | `name`, `content`, `reference`, text `metadata.<key>` | `content contains "late fee"` |
| `startswith` | Begins with the text | Same | `name startswith "contract-"` |
| `endswith` | Ends with the text | Same | `name endswith ".pdf"` |

These operators match literally, without wildcards: `%` and `_` match only themselves. They do not split words or match synonyms. Use the search terms for meaning and the filter for exact constraints.

### Lists

| Operator | Meaning | Fields | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `in` | Equals any value in the list | `name`, `content`, `reference`, `tags`, `metadata.<key>` | `metadata.region in ("latam", "emea")` |
| `has` | The list contains the value | `tags`, array `metadata.<key>` | `tags has "finance"` |

`field in (a, b, c)` is equivalent to `field = a or field = b or field = c`. For `tags`, `in` matches documents that have at least one of the listed tags. `has` is the only equality-style operator for `tags`; `tags = "x"` is rejected.

### Existence

| Operator | Meaning | Fields | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exists` | The metadata key is present, even when its value is `null` | `metadata.<key>` | `metadata.reviewer exists` |

`exists` takes no value. To require a non-null value, combine it with `!=`: `metadata.reviewer exists and metadata.reviewer != null`.

## Values

### Strings

Strings use double or single quotes. Inside a string, escape the same quote with a backslash: `"say \"hi\""`, `'it\'s'`. Supported escapes are `\"`, `\'`, `\\`, `\/`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, and `\uXXXX`.

Text comparisons ignore letter case and accents: `name = "relatorio"` matches a document named `Relatório`. `=` and `in` also ignore trailing spaces: `"report "` matches `"report"`.

### Numbers

Numbers use a dot as the decimal separator and may use an exponent: `10`, `-2.5`, `1e3`. Numbers are never quoted; `"100"` is a string.

### Booleans and null

`true`, `false`, and `null` are literals, written without quotes. They are valid only for `metadata.<key>`.

### Dates

`createdAt` and `updatedAt` accept absolute dates and relative times.

**Absolute dates** use ISO 8601 inside quotes:

```text
createdAt >= "2026-09-01"
updatedAt < "2026-09-01T18:30"
createdAt >= "2026-09-01T00:00:00-03:00"
createdAt >= "2026-09-01T03:00:00Z"
```

- A date without a time means midnight.
- A value without `Z` or an offset is interpreted in the AIVAX service time zone, America/Sao_Paulo (UTC−03:00). Add `Z` or an offset when you need an exact instant.
- Other formats, such as `15/06/2025`, are rejected.

**Relative times** use `now`, optionally followed by `+` or `-` and an amount with a unit, without quotes:

| Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `m` | minutes |
| `h` | hours |
| `d` | days |
| `w` | weeks |
| `mo` | calendar months |
| `y` | calendar years |

```text
createdAt >= now-7d
updatedAt >= now-12h and updatedAt < now
```

`now` is valid only in date conditions.

### Lists

A list is one or more values separated by commas inside parentheses: `("finance", "legal")`, `(2026, "2026")`. Lists are used with `in`.

## Combining Conditions

Join conditions with `and`, `or`, and `not`:

```text
not tags has "draft"
tags has "finance" and createdAt >= now-30d
(tags has "finance" or tags has "legal") and updatedAt >= "2026-01-01"
```

`not` binds tighter than `and`, and `and` binds tighter than `or`. So `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`. Use parentheses to group explicitly.

## Metadata

Use a dot to read nested metadata. Keys that are not simple identifiers go in quotes:

```text
metadata.author.name = "Ana"
metadata."file-path" startswith "/contracts/2026/"
metadata."a.b" = 1
```

The last example reads one key named `a.b`, not a nested path. Array indexes are not supported; use `has` to check whether an array contains a value.

**Types are never converted.** The literal type selects which stored values can match:

| Literal | Matches stored values of type |
| --- | --- |
| text | JSON string |
| number | JSON number |
| `true` / `false` | JSON boolean |
| `null` | JSON `null` |

So `metadata.year = 2026` does not match `{"year": "2026"}`, and `metadata.public = true` does not match `{"public": "true"}`. If your data mixes types, list both: `metadata.year in (2026, "2026")`.

Ordering operators work only on numbers in metadata. Dates stored in metadata cannot be compared as dates; use `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, or store a sortable number such as a Unix timestamp or `20260915`.

A missing key never matches a positive condition, so `metadata.lang != "en"` also matches documents without `lang`. To exclude them, add `metadata.lang exists`.

Store metadata with consistent types per key, and prefer keys made of ASCII letters, digits, `-`, and `_`.

## Examples

| Goal | Filter |
| --- | --- |
| Documents with a tag | `tags has "finance"` |
| Any of several tags | `tags in ("finance", "legal")` |
| Exclude drafts | `not tags has "draft"` |
| A specific document | `name = "refund-policy"` |
| Documents from one family | `name startswith "manual-v2-"` |
| All chunks of one source | `reference = "manual-v2"` |
| Content mentioning a term | `content contains "late fee"` |
| Created in the last 30 days | `createdAt >= now-30d` |
| Updated in September 2026 | `updatedAt >= "2026-09-01" and updatedAt < "2026-10-01"` |
| One metadata value | `metadata.department = "finance"` |
| Several metadata values | `metadata.author.name in ("Ana", "Bruno")` |
| Numeric range | `metadata.pages > 10 and metadata.pages <= 200` |
| Boolean flag | `metadata.public = true` |
| Metadata array contains | `metadata.languages has "pt-BR"` |
| Key present and not null | `metadata.reviewer exists and metadata.reviewer != null` |
| Key absent | `not metadata.archived exists` |
| Combined | `(tags has "finance" or metadata.department = "finance") and createdAt >= now-1mo` |

## Common Mistakes

| Instead of | Write |
| --- | --- |
| `name == "x"` | `name = "x"` |
| `lower(name) = "x"` | `name = "x"` (already case-insensitive) |
| `tags = "x"` | `tags has "x"` |
| `metadata.price > "100"` | `metadata.price > 100`, with the price stored as a number |
| `createdAt >= "15/06/2025"` | `createdAt >= "2025-06-15"` |
| `metadata.date >= "2025-06-15"` | `createdAt >= "2025-06-15"`, or a numeric metadata value |
| `content contains "ai"` | A term with at least 3 characters |
| `"filters": [ ... ]` | `"filter": [ ... ]` |

## Where Filters Are Supported

Send the filter in the `filter` field of these endpoints:

- [Query collections, Find similar documents, and Browse documents](../rag/semantic-search.md)
- Answer generation

The field accepts a string or an array of strings. Array items are combined with `and`:

```json
{
  "terms": "How do I request a refund?",
  "collections": [ "<collection-id>" ],
  "filter": [
    "tags has \"billing\"",
    "metadata.region = \"latam\""
  ]
}
```

The search endpoints also accept a filter for a single collection, combined with the top-level `filter` for that collection:

```json
{
  "terms": "How do I request a refund?",
  "collections": [
    "<collection-id>",
    { "id": "<other-collection-id>", "filter": "metadata.source = \"crm\"" }
  ],
  "filter": "tags has \"billing\""
}
```

A missing or `null` field means no filter. The field name is `filter`; other names, such as `filters`, are ignored and the search runs without a filter.

Models can also send a filter string in the optional `filter` argument of these tools:

- The search tool of the [Collections MCP](../mcp-utilities/collections-mcp.md#generated-tools).
- The `query` tool of AI gateways that use the `QueryFunction` [query strategy](../inference/pipelines.md).

The [`memory_search` tool](../tools/builtin-tools.md#search-memories) also accepts a filter string, but requires exactly one of `query` or `filter`, not both. Its filter-only mode returns up to 10 matching memories for the current user, newest first, without query embeddings.

Automatic gateway RAG, which searches before the model call, does not apply filters. An invalid filter in a tool call is returned to the model as a tool error with the same message as the API.

## Limits

These limits apply to every filter, including filters used by memory search and the Collections MCP.

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Filter length | 2,048 characters per string |
| Conditions | 32 per string |
| Nesting of parentheses and `not` | 8 levels |
| Values in one `in` list | 100 |
| Length of a text value or metadata key | 256 characters |
| Keys in a metadata path | 8 |
| Minimum `contains` length | 3 characters |
| Execution time | 10 seconds |

Conditions on `content`, `endswith`, tags, and metadata examine every document in the requested collections, so they take longer in large collections. If a filter exceeds the time limit, the request fails and asks for more selective conditions. Prefer conditions on `name` (`=`, `in`, `startswith`), split very large corpora into smaller collections, and reserve `content contains` for collections where it stays fast.

## Errors

An invalid filter returns `400 Bad Request` with a message that names the problem and the character position where it was found:

```json
{
  "error": "Invalid filter: Unknown field 'author'. Expected name, content, reference, tags, createdAt, updatedAt or metadata.<key>. (at 0)"
}
```

For an array, the message includes the index of the invalid item, such as `Invalid filter at index 1: ...`. A `filter` that is not a string or an array of strings is also rejected.

# Documents

A document is the unit that AIVAX indexes and retrieves inside a [collection](collections.md). Each document stores text, an optional reference, optional tags, optional metadata, and the vectors generated by the indexing job. Search quality depends heavily on how clear, focused, and self-contained each document is.

## Anatomy of a document

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Name | Required stable identifier, up to 256 characters. Existing documents are matched by name, so reuse the same name to update a document. |
| Contents | Required text that is embedded and searched semantically. |
| Reference | Optional ID, up to 64 characters, that groups chunks belonging to the same logical source. |
| Tags | Optional labels for filtering, browsing, and maintenance. |
| Metadata | Optional object returned with results, such as source URL, version, author, or publication date. |

Only the contents are embedded. Metadata and tags are returned with results and can be used in [advanced filters](document-filters.md), but they do not influence semantic matching. If users may search for "refund policy", those words must appear in the contents, not only in a tag.

Use references when several documents represent parts of the same source, such as sections of a contract, clauses of a policy, or chunks of a PDF. When a search enables reference expansion, a matched document can bring the other documents that share its reference.

## Write good documents

A document should represent one limited piece of knowledge. As a practical target, keep most documents between 20 and 700 words. This is not an API rule, but it usually gives the embedding model enough context without mixing unrelated topics. Split longer content at logical boundaries such as sections, clauses, FAQ entries, or product descriptions.

Do:

- Give each document a clear name and focused text.
- Put the subject near the start of the document.
- Use natural language similar to the way users ask questions.
- Repeat important identifiers, product names, policy names, acronyms, and terms when they matter.
- Include enough context for the text to be understood on its own.

Avoid:

- Empty, tiny, or title-only documents.
- Entire PDFs, chapters, logs, or manuals as one document.
- Multiple unrelated subjects in one document.
- Text that depends on surrounding pages to make sense.
- Mixed languages inside the same document, unless users are expected to search that way.
- Raw JSON, code, tables, or logs without a short natural-language explanation.
- Pronouns such as "it" or "the product" when the document does not identify the subject.

For example, prefer:

```text
The color of the 2015 Honda Civic registered in fleet record CAR-123 is yellow.
```

over:

```text
The car is yellow.
```

The first version can be retrieved and understood without external context.

### Chunking larger sources

When importing PDFs, spreadsheets, web pages, or manuals, inspect the resulting chunks before relying on the collection. Remove repeated headers, footers, navigation menus, broken tables, boilerplate, and irrelevant disclaimers when possible. A good chunk includes a title or source heading, the immediate section context, and the complete rule, answer, or explanation. A poor chunk contains half of a table row, a sentence that depends on the previous page, or several policies mixed together. [Text Segmentation](../data-processing/text-segmentation.md) can split source text into cohesive segments before import.

### Document size

Very small documents, below about 32 tokens, are accepted but may not be retrieved reliably. Documents above about 4,096 tokens are accepted and indexed, but they record a warning in the account logs because a single vector represents their whole text less precisely. Text far beyond that size is truncated for embedding. Split large documents instead of relying on truncation.

## Import documents

AIVAX supports several ways to add documents. All of them queue new or changed documents for indexing; a document becomes searchable after its state changes from **Queued** to **Indexed**.

| Method | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| Create or update one document | Your application manages documents one at a time, such as an admin screen that saves one FAQ entry. |
| Batch import over WebSocket | You have many prepared documents, such as chunks generated from PDFs, catalogs, policies, or help-center articles. |
| Import from files with Media Injector | You have source files whose knowledge has not yet been split into retrieval-ready text. |

### Updates and reindexing

Documents are matched by name. When a document is created, it is queued for indexing. When its contents change, it is queued again and its vectors are regenerated. Unchanged documents are skipped.

The single-document update can change the reference, tags, or metadata without reindexing, and fields omitted from it keep their current values. A batch import updates metadata alone without reindexing, but updates the reference and tags only together with changed contents; a line that changes only the reference or tags is skipped.

> [!WARNING]
> Indexing incurs cost based on document text tokens when documents are created or when their contents change.

### Batch import

Use the **Index Documents (JSONL WebSocket)** endpoint for batch imports. It replaces the multipart **Index Documents (JSONL)** upload, which remains available only for existing integrations. The WebSocket import streams documents in blocks, reports progress as it goes, accepts 10× the per-request document limit of the multipart upload, and lets you resume from the last committed line after a disconnection.

Each JSONL line represents one document:

| Property | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docid` | Yes | Document name. Existing documents are matched by this value. |
| `text` | Yes | Contents to index. |
| `__ref` | No | Reference ID. |
| `__tags` | No | Tags. |
| `__meta` | No | Metadata object. |

The import works as follows:

1. Open a WebSocket to the endpoint. Browsers can authenticate with the `api-key` query parameter. Add `insert-mode=sync` to delete collection documents whose names were not sent.
2. Send UTF-8 text messages with complete JSONL lines separated by `\n`. A message can contain one or many lines. Each message must arrive within 30 seconds of the previous one.
3. AIVAX commits the lines in blocks. For each block it checks the account balance, storage quota, and collection access, saves the documents, queues them for indexing, and sends a `progress` message with the number of committed lines.
4. Send a line containing only `END`. AIVAX saves the remaining lines, applies `insert-mode=sync` when requested, and sends a `completed` message before closing the connection.

If the connection closes, times out, or fails before `END`, uncommitted lines are discarded, while committed blocks remain queued. The `error` message reports the committed line count, so you can resend only the remaining lines. Only one import runs per collection at a time; a second import waits up to 30 seconds and then fails with `409 Conflict`.

When a line changes the text of an existing document, its reference and tags are replaced by the values sent; an omitted `__meta` keeps the existing metadata.

### Import from files with Media Injector

Media Injector turns a source file into focused, self-contained documents. It examines the source, identifies materially useful knowledge, writes concise factual documents in the source's predominant language, and queues them for indexing. Use direct import instead when you need exact source wording, deterministic boundaries, stable document names, or application-controlled metadata.

Media Injector is useful for PDFs that contain several independent topics, images or scanned pages whose visible content should become searchable, and audio or video whose facts should be available through RAG. It does not preserve the source as one searchable document. Review the generated documents when wording, coverage, legal fidelity, or sensitive-data handling is important.

In the Console:

1. Open the target collection and choose **Import from files**.
2. Select one or more source files.
3. Optionally provide processing context. The same context is applied to every selected file.
4. Confirm the import. The files are uploaded sequentially, and a separate job is created for each file after all of its chunks have reached AIVAX.
5. Follow the jobs under **Batch > Media Processing**.
6. After each job completes, review the generated documents and wait for indexing before testing [Search](semantic-search.md).

A job can be `queued`, `processing`, `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`. Failed or cancelled jobs can be retried while their uploaded data is still available. If no job appears, the upload did not reach its completion step; retry the upload and check the error shown. File names are preserved during upload, including accented letters and non-Latin scripts.

| Source group | Processing behavior |
| --- | --- |
| PDF documents | Reads document structure, text, and relevant visual content. |
| Images | Interprets visible text and content. |
| Audio | Interprets spoken and other relevant audible content; large files are segmented automatically. |
| Video | Interprets relevant visual and audible content; large files are segmented automatically. |

Use the original, accurate file extension, because it identifies the media type. If an audio or video file fails, convert it to a common format and retry.

**Processing context** is an optional instruction that helps Media Injector decide which facts are most valuable. It is not treated as a factual source and cannot add facts that are absent from the file. Describe the source's identity and purpose, the audience, the topics that matter, ambiguous terminology, and content to deprioritize:

```text
This is the 2026 support policy for Acme Cloud customers in Brazil. Prioritize eligibility rules, deadlines, plan differences, exceptions, and the steps a support agent must communicate. Ignore repeated page headers and signature blocks.
```

Do not ask it to infer conclusions, supply missing information, or calculate values the source does not report.

Generated documents prioritize source identity, scope, principal facts, relationships, and exceptions; combine closely related facts; ignore decorative text and pagination; and preserve the source's language, terminology, dates, and number formats. They are tagged as automatically produced content and indexed like other documents. Inspect documents generated from tables, scans, and repeated layouts before relying on them in production.

## Manage documents

You can manage documents in the Console, on the collection's **Browse documents** tab, or through the API. Management capabilities include:

- **Browse and filter** by tag, reference, content, name, or ID, by indexing state (queued or indexed), and sorted by creation, update, or indexing date.
- **Inspect** a document's contents, reference, tags, metadata, timestamps, and approximate token count. The Console editor also warns when a document has too many or too few words.
- **Edit** contents, reference, tags, and metadata. Changing the contents reindexes the document.
- **Delete** individual documents, or remove documents that were not sent in a synchronized batch import with `insert-mode=sync`.
- **Export** all documents of a collection as JSONL.
- **Remove duplicates** with the [collection de-duplicator](collections.md#de-duplicator).

See the Documents and Collections groups of the [API reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs) for the endpoints, including **Create or Update Document**, **Browse Documents**, **Get Document**, **Delete Document**, and **Export Collection**.

## Troubleshoot retrieval

When search results are poor, check the basics first:

- Confirm the documents are indexed.
- Test the collection with [Search](semantic-search.md) or the Console playground before testing through an AI Gateway.
- Try a complete question instead of isolated keywords, and compare the query language with the document language.
- Review whether the answer is split across too many small documents or buried inside a very large one.
- Check search history and query coverage in [RAG Observability](observability.md).

## Pricing and limits

Document indexing is billed as collection text embedding; see [Collections](collections.md#pricing-and-limits). Media Injector is billed for input, cached input, output, and media usage of the processing job, in addition to the normal embedding cost of the generated documents. Rates depend on media type and input-token volume.

| Media Injector | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| PDFs and images - up to 272K input tokens | Input **$0.30/M tokens**; cache **$0.03/M tokens**; output **$1.80/M tokens** |
| PDFs and images - above 272K input tokens | Input **$0.60/M tokens**; cache **$0.06/M tokens**; output **$3.60/M tokens** |
| Audio - up to 256K input tokens | Input/media **$0.60/M tokens**; cache **$0.12/M tokens**; output **$3.00/M tokens** |
| Audio - above 256K input tokens | Input/media **$1.20/M tokens**; cache **$0.24/M tokens**; output **$6.00/M tokens** |
| Video | Input/media **$0.45/M tokens**; cache **$0.045/M tokens**; output **$3.75/M tokens** |

| Limit | Free | Pro | Max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Document insertions | 500/day | 10,000/day | — |
| Documents per multipart JSONL import | 1,000 | 10,000 | 1,000,000 |
| Documents per WebSocket JSONL import | 10,000 | 100,000 | 10,000,000 |
| Media Injector | 2 files/day | 30 files/day | 1,000 files/day |

An em dash (`—`) means the plan does not impose a limit. If an import exceeds the per-import limit, split it into multiple imports. If the account reaches the daily insertion limit, wait for the window to reset or upgrade the plan.

# RAG Observability

The [AIVAX Console](https://console.aivax.net) shows how your collections are indexed, which searches they receive, and how well those searches score. Use it to confirm that an import finished, find questions your knowledge base answers poorly, and spot content that is never retrieved.

## Collections overview

Open **RAG Collections** in the Console sidebar. Each collection shows its **Current state** as a bar with three parts:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Indexed | Documents that are searchable with the collection's current embedding model. |
| Queued | Documents waiting for indexing. They are not searchable yet. |
| Outdated | Documents indexed with a different embedding model than the collection's current one. They remain searchable, but their vectors may be less accurate. |

A large Queued share after an import is normal and decreases as indexing proceeds. If Outdated documents remain, use **Update outdated documents** in the collection settings to regenerate their vectors; see [Maintain a collection](collections.md#maintain-a-collection).

## Collection health

Select **View** on a collection to open its **Browse documents** tab. The cards at the top summarize the collection:

| Card | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Total documents | All documents in the collection, queued and indexed. |
| Query coverage | Percentage of documents that appeared in at least one search result among the recorded searches. A low value means much of the content is never retrieved. |
| Avg. Performance | Average processing time of a search, in milliseconds. |
| Avg. Score | Average score of the returned results, from 0 to 1. Higher is better. |

Low query coverage is not always a problem: a broad knowledge base can contain content that users rarely ask about. It deserves attention when documents you expect to be used never appear, which often points to documents that are too long, mixed-topic, or written differently from how users ask.

The document list below the cards shows each document's state, tags, reference, and token count, and can be filtered by state. Open **Details** on a document to see its timestamps, including when it was last indexed, and its character, word, and approximate token counts. The document editor warns when a document has too many or too few words for reliable retrieval; see [Write good documents](documents.md#write-good-documents).

## Search history

The **Transactions** tab lists the searches performed on the collection, including searches made by AI Gateways, MCP clients, and your applications. Searches are kept for 2 hours on Free, 7 days on Pro, and 30 days on Max.

Use the **View** selector to choose what to review:

- **Recent** shows the newest searches.
- **Low quality** shows the lowest-scoring searches. Start here to find questions the collection answers poorly.
- **High quality** shows the highest-scoring searches.

Each search shows its moment, query, number of results, and three scores:

| Score | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Original score | Vector similarity between the query and the documents, before reranking. |
| Reranker score | Score assigned by the reranker, with the reranker name. A dash means no reranker was used. |
| Final score | Score used to rank the results. |

Open **Details** on a search to see its processing time, cost, scores, and the documents it returned, each with its original, reranker, and final score and a preview of the text. A document that was later deleted is shown as no longer existing.

### Diagnose a low-quality search

1. Read the query and compare it with the returned documents. If the right document is absent, the problem is retrieval, not ranking.
2. If the right document exists but scored low, check whether its text uses the same terms and language as the query, and whether it mixes several topics.
3. If the original score is good but the final score drops, compare rerankers; see [Rerankers](reranking.md).
4. If no document covers the question, add the missing knowledge to the collection.

## Test searches in the playground

Select **Playground** on a collection to run a search without writing code. Set the search text, minimum score, maximum results, reranker, reference expansion, and [advanced filters](document-filters.md), then select **Run query**. The **Visual** tab shows the ranked documents with their scores, contents, and metadata, and the generated answer when you use answer generation; the **JSON** tab shows the raw result.

Use the playground to reproduce a low-quality search from the history, adjust options, and confirm an improvement before changing an AI Gateway. For processing time, cost, and per-stage scores, use the search details in **Transactions**.

## Media Injector jobs

Files imported with [Media Injector](documents.md#import-from-files-with-media-injector) are processed as background jobs. Follow them under **Batch > Media Processing**, which refreshes automatically and shows each job's collection, files, state, elapsed time, number of documents produced, current cost, and estimated cost. Cancel queued or processing jobs, and retry or delete failed or cancelled ones.

After a job completes, its documents appear in the collection as Queued until they are indexed.

## Cost and storage

- **Analytics > Usage per resource** groups usage by resource, including each collection, and links to it.
- **Analytics > Monthly Reports** shows the month's RAG cost, which includes embeddings, queries, and reranking.
- **Usage and limits** shows storage used against your plan quota.

De-duplication runs report their result through account notifications; see [De-duplicator](collections.md#de-duplicator).

# Reflex

Reflex is AIVAX's collection-less search for RAG. Send a query together with candidate document strings and receive the most relevant items in ranked order—without indexing, storing, or maintaining a RAG collection first.

Reflex is the default ranker of the autonomous [reranking endpoint](reranking.md): calling that endpoint without a `model` selects Reflex. This page explains when to choose Reflex; the reranking page covers candidate preparation and ranker comparison in depth.

Use Reflex when your application already owns the candidate documents, the candidate set changes frequently, or you want a retrieval step without collection indexing and storage. Use [Semantic Search](semantic-search.md) when AIVAX should store, index, and search a persistent knowledge base or narrow a corpus that is too large to submit as candidates on every request.

## Reflex or Semantic Search?

| Choose Reflex when... | Choose Semantic Search when... |
| --- | --- |
| Your application already has the candidate document strings. | Documents should live in managed AIVAX collections. |
| You need retrieval immediately, without an indexing step. | The knowledge base is persistent and searched repeatedly. |
| The candidate set is dynamic or request-specific. | The corpus is too large to submit as candidates on every request. |
| You want collection-less ranking. | You want collection filtering, stored metadata, document references, and managed retrieval. |

Reflex returns ranked text candidates; it does not generate an answer. Pass the selected documents to your language model or AI Gateway as RAG context. To decide between Reflex and a cross-encoder reranker, see [reranking RAG results without a cross-encoder](https://aivax.net/blog/reflex-retrieval-built-for-recurring-documents/).

## Use Reflex

Call the reranking API with a query and the candidate documents your application wants to compare. Results are returned in relevance order. Each result keeps its input position, so you can map it back to your application data.

Use concise, focused candidate documents. Reranking can improve their order, but it cannot recover information that was not included in the candidates. If the expected document is consistently absent, improve candidate selection, chunking, or query formulation before tuning the ranker.

Reflex limits the number of candidate documents per request and the number of ranked results returned; see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits). If your candidate pool exceeds the candidate limit, narrow it first — with lexical pre-filtering, a cheap first-pass rank, or collection retrieval — and let Reflex order the shortlist.

For the supported request, response, authentication, and error contract, use the API Reference:

## Use Reflex with RAG

Reflex is also the default reranker after AIVAX retrieves candidates from RAG collections. In this flow, it can improve the order of retrieved candidates but cannot recover a document that the retrieval stage did not select. If relevant documents are consistently absent, adjust retrieval, chunking, query formulation, or candidate count before tuning reranking.

Free, Pro, and Max include a daily reranking allowance for Reflex, shared between autonomous calls and RAG reranking. Cached and uncached input both consume this allowance. It is separate from the RAG embedding allowance and the processing-time cap; other rerankers are billed normally. For relative plan capacity and coverage rules, see [Plans and Limits](../limits.md#included-daily-subscription-allowances).

## Pricing and limits

Reflex is billed by input tokens. Input served from the account-scoped cache is billed at a lower rate. Accounts with [Data Sharing](../data-sharing.md) enabled receive a discount on eligible reranking operations.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Reflex - cache miss | **$0.015/M tokens** |
| Reflex - cache hit | **$0.003/M tokens** |

| Limit | Free | Pro | Max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reflex processing time | 30 minutes/day | 6 hours/day | — |
| Reranking requests | 30/min | 1,000/min | — |
| Candidate documents per request | 10,000 | 10,000 | 10,000 |
| Ranked results returned | 200 | 200 | 200 |

The processing-time limit counts the time spent processing Reflex requests, both on the reranking endpoint and in RAG searches that use Reflex; cached input does not consume it separately. The reranking request limit applies to the reranking endpoint and to RAG searches that use a reranker, including searches through AI Gateways and MCP tools. An em dash (`—`) means the plan does not impose a limit. Requests above a limit return `429 Too Many Requests`.

# Rerankers

Rerankers reorder an existing set of candidate documents for a query. They do not search a collection or recover text that is absent from the input. Use the autonomous reranking API when your application already owns the candidates, or use [Semantic Search](semantic-search.md) to retrieve candidates from an AIVAX collection before reranking them.

[Reflex](reflex.md) is the default ranker of this endpoint and AIVAX's collection-less search experience. See that page when you want retrieval-style ranking without managing a collection.

## Rerank documents directly

Authenticate with an [AIVAX API key](../authentication.md) and send a query with the candidate document strings. The API returns the candidates in relevance order. Each result keeps its input position, so you can map it back to your application data.

Use direct reranking when candidates are dynamic, come from another search system, or do not need to be stored in an AIVAX collection. Use managed semantic search when AIVAX should retrieve candidates from a persistent corpus.

For the supported request, response, authentication, and error contract, use the API Reference:

## Build candidates worth ranking

Reranking only reorders what it receives, so candidate quality decides the ceiling. Keep each candidate string focused on one idea — a paragraph or a short section rather than a whole page — so the relevance score reflects one topic instead of an average over many. When candidates come from chunking, prefer boundaries that preserve complete statements; see [Text segmentation](../data-processing/text-segmentation.md).

Use the [RAG pipeline checklist](https://aivax.net/blog/a-vector-database-is-not-a-rag-system/) to distinguish preparation, retrieval, and ordering failures.

Send enough candidates to cover plausible answers: over-retrieve first, then rank precisely. Use `top_n` to keep only the head of the ranked list, and `min_score` to drop low-relevance tail results. Calibrate that threshold on your own queries, because score scales differ between rankers and a cutoff tuned on one workload rarely transfers to another.

## Choosing a reranker

Start with the default reranker unless you have a measured reason to select another available option. The default is Reflex; alternatives include lexical matching, reciprocal-rank fusion of several signals, and third-party cross-encoders. Fusion (`rrf`) is retrieval-only and is rejected by this endpoint: it exists for combining signals inside collection search, not for autonomous ranking.

To compare options, fix a set of representative queries with known relevant documents from your own workload — covering your languages, document lengths, and jargon — and measure whether swapping rankers moves the right document upward. If the relevant document is missing from the candidates entirely, no ranker can recover it; improve candidate retrieval, chunking, query formulation, or candidate count before comparing rerankers.

To separate missing-candidate failures from poor-ordering failures before you add a reranker, see [Do I need a reranker for RAG?](https://aivax.net/blog/semantic-search-vs-reranking/). To judge when Reflex is enough compared with a cross-encoder, see [reranking RAG results without a cross-encoder](https://aivax.net/blog/reflex-retrieval-built-for-recurring-documents/).

For current availability, supported options, and account limits, see the API Reference and [Plans and Limits](../limits.md).

# Search

AIVAX searches the indexed documents of one or more collections through three endpoints:

| Endpoint | Path | Use it to | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Query collections | `POST /api/v2/query` | Find the documents that best answer a question. | Query embedding and, when used, reranking. |
| Find similar documents | `POST /api/v2/query/similar` | Find documents close in meaning to a document you already have. | No embedding or reranking cost. |
| Browse documents | `POST /api/v2/query/browse` | List documents in a fixed order, optionally filtered, without relevance. | No embedding or reranking cost. |

RAG answer generation and collections attached to an AI Gateway use the same retrieval engine.

If your application already owns the candidate document strings, consider [Reflex](reflex.md): a collection-less search that ranks supplied documents without indexing or storage. Use managed search when AIVAX should store and search a persistent corpus or when the corpus is too large to submit as candidates with every request.

Before searching, add [documents](documents.md) to a [collection](collections.md) and wait for indexing. Only indexed documents are returned. Compare [vector search with the complete RAG pipeline](https://aivax.net/blog/a-vector-database-is-not-a-rag-system/) before deciding what to build.

## Query collections

A query runs in this order:

1. If a filter is set, AIVAX restricts each collection to the documents that match it.
2. Each search term is embedded and compared with the remaining documents.
3. Documents below `minScore` are discarded, and the closest `candidates` documents form the candidate pool.
4. The reranker reorders the pool, unless reranking is disabled.
5. The pool is sorted and returned in pages of `limit` results.

```json
{
  "collections": [ "<collection-id>" ],
  "terms": "How do I request a refund?"
}
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `collections` | Required | Collection IDs owned by the account. An item can also be `{ "id": "<collection-id>", "filter": "..." }` to filter only that collection. |
| `terms` | Required | One search text or a list of alternative texts. |
| `filter` | — | An [advanced filter](document-filters.md) expression, or a list of expressions that must all match. |
| `minScore` | 0.2 | Minimum vector similarity, from 0 to 0.99, for a document to enter the candidate pool. Raise it to drop weak matches; lower it when relevant documents are missing. |
| `candidates` | `limit` × 3 | Size of the candidate pool, from `limit` to 1000. A larger pool gives the reranker and later pages more documents to work with. |
| `reranker` | `smart` (Reflex) | Reranker that orders the pool: `smart`, `lexical`, `rrf`, `none`, or a full reranker name. See [Rerankers](reranking.md). |
| `sort` | Score, descending | `{ "by": "score" \| "createdAt" \| "updatedAt" \| "indexedAt" \| "name", "dir": "asc" \| "desc" }`. Without `dir`, score sorts descending and the other fields ascending. |
| `limit` | 10 | Results per page, from 1 to 128. |
| `cursor` | — | `page.cursor` from the previous response, to read the next page. |
| `include` | `content`, `metadata` | Optional document fields: `content`, `metadata`, and `references`. `references` attaches the other documents that share the reference of each result. |

### Sorting and reranking

A reranker orders by relevance, so it only applies when results are sorted by score:

| Request | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| No `sort` and no `reranker` | Reflex reranks the pool; results are sorted by score. |
| `reranker` without `sort` | That reranker reranks the pool; results are sorted by score. |
| `sort` other than score, without `reranker` | Reranking is disabled. The pool is selected by similarity and then sorted by the requested field. |
| `sort` other than score with `reranker: "none"` | Same as above. |
| `sort` other than score with any other `reranker` | Rejected with `400 Bad Request`. |

To get the most recent relevant documents, select a pool by meaning and sort it by date:

```json
{
  "collections": [ "<collection-id>" ],
  "terms": "pricing change",
  "candidates": 100,
  "sort": { "by": "createdAt", "dir": "desc" }
}
```

Each reranker has a maximum number of documents it accepts; a `candidates` value above it is rejected.

### Results

Each result has a `rank`, a `document`, and `scores`:

- `document` contains `id`, `collectionId`, `name`, `reference`, `tags`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `indexedAt`, and the fields requested in `include`.
- `scores.similarity` is the vector similarity, `scores.rerank` is the reranker score (or `null`), and `scores.final` is the rerank score when a reranker ran, otherwise the similarity.

The response also contains `page.cursor`, `page.hasMore`, `page.candidates` (the size of the pool), and the `reranker` that ran.

### Pages

The first request computes the candidate pool and returns its first page. To read the next page, send the same request body with `cursor` set to the previous `page.cursor`. Later pages are read from the stored pool, so they are not charged again and keep the same order.

A cursor expires after 10 minutes without use and then returns `410 Gone`; repeat the request without `cursor` to run the query again. A cursor sent with a different request body is rejected with `400 Bad Request`. The pool never grows: to see more than `candidates` results, raise `candidates`.

## Find similar documents

Find similar documents uses the stored vector of an indexed document as the query, as in a "more like this" feature. The source document is never returned. It accepts `documentId` and the same `collections`, `filter`, `minScore`, `candidates`, `sort`, `limit`, `cursor`, and `include` options as a query; without `collections`, it searches the collection of the source document.

```json
{
  "documentId": "<document-id>",
  "limit": 5
}
```

Nothing is embedded or reranked, so `scores.rerank` is always `null`. The source document must be indexed; a document still waiting for indexing is rejected with `400 Bad Request`.

## Browse documents

Browse documents lists indexed documents without semantic search. By default, documents are returned in insertion order, oldest first. Without a filter, every indexed document of the collections is listed.

```json
{
  "collections": [ "<collection-id>" ],
  "filter": "createdAt >= now-7d",
  "sort": { "by": "createdAt", "dir": "desc" },
  "limit": 50
}
```

It accepts `collections`, `filter`, `sort`, `limit`, `cursor`, and `include`. `sort.by` can be `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `indexedAt`, or `name`; sorting by score is rejected. Results contain only `document`, without `rank` or `scores`.

Browse cursors point to the last returned document instead of a stored pool, so they do not expire. Documents added or changed between requests appear in later pages according to the sort order.

## Filter results

Filters narrow the documents a search can return, using exact conditions on document fields rather than semantic similarity. Use them when the answer must come from a known subset, such as one product, tenant, language, document type, or period.

| Filter on | Example | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | `name startswith "policy-"` | Document families that follow a naming convention. |
| Tags | `tags has "finance"` | Operational labels assigned on import. |
| Metadata | `metadata.region = "br"` | Structured values stored with each document, such as region, version, or author. |
| Contents | `content contains "refund"` | Required words or identifiers in the text. |
| Dates | `updatedAt >= now-30d` | Recently created or updated documents. |

Combine conditions with `and`, `or`, `not`, and parentheses, for example `tags has "finance" and createdAt >= now-30d`. When `filter` is a list, every expression must match. A filter set on a collection item is combined with the top-level `filter` for that collection.

Filters are evaluated before the search terms are embedded. Only matching documents are ranked, so results never include documents outside the filter. When no document matches, a query returns an empty result without generating embeddings or charging for the query.

Filters do not replace good document text: the meaning a user searches for must appear in the contents. See [Advanced filters](document-filters.md) for the complete syntax, operators, limits, and errors, or [How to filter RAG results by metadata, tags and date](https://aivax.net/blog/filter-rag-results-by-metadata-tags-date/) for a worked guide.

## Multiple terms

Multiple terms cover alternative retrieval paths rather than requiring every term to match the same document. Each document is scored by its best match among the terms. Use them for synonyms, alternative phrasings, or several acceptable ways to find an answer.

If the user's question combines several related conditions, keep them together in one search term. For example, prefer:

```text
How do I cancel an annual subscription without a penalty?
```

Over disconnected keywords:

```text
cancellation
annual subscription
penalty
```

A complete query usually performs better than a list of disconnected keywords because it preserves the relationship between concepts. If users search by product codes, policy IDs, plan names, or procedure names, include those identifiers in the document text.

## Reranking

A reranker adjusts the order of the candidate pool returned by vector search. It does not search additional documents or recover text that the retrieval stage did not select; raise `candidates` to give it more documents. See [Rerankers](reranking.md) for selection guidance.

## Errors

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400 Bad Request` | Invalid field, unknown collection or document, [invalid filter](document-filters.md#errors), a reranker combined with a sort other than score, or a cursor sent with a different request body. |
| `410 Gone` | The query cursor expired. Repeat the request without `cursor`. |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | The plan's search or reranking rate limit was exceeded. |

## Search quality

If search returns poor results:

1. Confirm that the documents are indexed.
2. Query the collection directly before testing through an AI Gateway.
3. Compare complete questions with alternative phrasings.
4. Check whether the relevant document is too short, too long, or not self-contained; see [Write good documents](documents.md#write-good-documents).
5. Check whether the query language matches the document language.
6. If the gateway rewrites questions before searching, test with the plain query path to isolate rewriting issues.
7. Review low-scoring searches and query coverage in [RAG Observability](observability.md).

To expose collections as tools for an external MCP client, see [Collections and RAG MCP](../mcp-utilities/collections-mcp.md). For search pricing and rate limits, see [Collections](collections.md#pricing-and-limits).

# Built-in Tools

AIVAX provides a list of built-in tools for you to enable in your model. These tools can be used together with the [server-side functions](/docs/tools/protocol-functions).

Some functions have usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling them in a production workflow.

Note that each model decides which function to call and its parameters. Not all models can obey the call rules.

## How to Choose and Combine Tools

Built-in tools should be enabled as work capabilities, not as agent decoration. Each tool adds a decision to the model: it needs to perceive that the tool exists, understand when to use it, assemble valid arguments, wait for the result, and continue the response. The more similar tools are available at the same time, the higher the chance of redundant use or poor choice. Start with the smallest set that solves the use case and write clear instructions on when to use each.

Use `WebSearch` when the answer depends on public, recent, or variable information. Use `OpenUrl` when the user has already provided a URL and wants the assistant to analyze that specific content. `AdvancedWebUsage` is disabled and returns an unavailable response; see [Changelogs](../legal/changelogs.md). Use `Code` for calculation, data transformation, and small algorithmic reasoning. Use `Request` when the model needs to call an HTTP API with method, headers, or custom body. Use `Remember` only in chat clients or calls with an identifiable user, because memory tools store and retrieve persistent information for that user.

Generation tools, such as image, document, and web page, should be treated as output actions. They do more than improve an answer; they create artifacts hosted or attached to the conversation. Therefore, instruct the model on when to generate an artifact and when to reply in text. In support, for example, generating a document can be useful for a quote, proposal, or formal summary; generating a web page can be useful for a visual report; generating an image can be useful for creative ideation. If the user only asked for an explanation, plain text is usually sufficient.

When tools are available via `builtin_tools` in a direct call, the application making the request decides the list for each inference. When configured in the AI Gateway, the list is centralized and can be combined with skills, workers, MCP, protocol functions, and shell. In production, prefer the gateway for permanent policies, because it prevents different clients from enabling different tools without control. Use direct calls for testing, internal routines, and flows where the application truly needs to choose tools dynamically.

The values in `builtin_tools.tools` are configuration flags such as `WebSearch`, `Code`, and `OpenUrl`. The model sees runtime function names such as `web_search`, `evaluate_code`, and `open_url`. Use runtime function names when configuring skill tool allowlists or shell tool allowlists.

text:
## Current Date and Time

Enable `DateTime` to expose `get_date_time`. This tool takes no arguments and reads the current time when it is called. It returns the date, time, day of the week, time zone, UTC offset, and an ISO 8601 timestamp.

The tool reports the gateway time zone, set in the gateway's `parameters.timeZone` with an IANA identifier. The default is `America/Sao_Paulo`, and daylight-saving changes are applied automatically. In the dashboard, edit **Time zone** under **Date and time** in the gateway's **Parameters + Tuning** tab. The same zone is used by scheduling tools and by the Bash tool, so every date the model reads or writes uses one time zone. The browser or user-context time zone does not change it.

To use another zone for a single request to `/v1/chat/completions`, send `time_zone`, such as `"time_zone": "Asia/Tokyo"`. Invalid identifiers are rejected. Batch workflows use the time zone of the AI Gateway they run on, or `America/Sao_Paulo` when they name a model directly.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": ["DateTime"]
}
```

For a saved gateway, include `DateTime` in `parameters.sentinelOptions.enabledFunctions`. For a Batch workflow, use `enabledTools.enabledFunctions`.

Example tool result (illustrative, not a live reading):

```json
{
    "date": "2026-07-15",
    "time": "09:30:00",
    "day_of_week": "Wednesday",
    "time_zone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "utc_offset": "-07:00",
    "date_time": "2026-07-15T09:30:00-07:00"
}
```

The date uses `yyyy-MM-dd`, time uses 24-hour `HH:mm:ss`, and weekday names are returned in English. All fields describe the same instant.

## Internet Search

This function enables internet search in your model. With this, the model can query specific or real‐time information such as weather data, news, game results, etc.

Internet search is performed by multiple providers, chosen based on network availability and latency. AIVAX uses a mix of providers to perform internet searches.

AIVAX provides two types of searches configurable via its dashboard:

- **Full**: the performed search is complete, inserting the entire content of each result into the conversation context.
- **Summarized**: the performed search is summarized, inserting into the conversation context a summary generated by AI by the search provider itself.

The `Full` mode may consume more input tokens from the conversation, but can provide more precise results. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling internet search in production.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Important:** the `Full` search is not always available.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "WebSearch"
    ],
    "options": {
        "web_search_max_results": 10,
        "web_search_mode": "full"
    }
}
```

## Advanced Internet Search

`AdvancedWebUsage` is disabled and returns an unavailable response. See [Changelogs](../legal/changelogs.md) for details.

## URL Context

This function allows the model to access external content at URLs and links provided by the user. With this function, the model can access links and evaluate their content.

Note that some destinations may identify the access as a bot and block it, as this function is not crawling but a simple GET to the destination.

Upon obtaining link content, the system checks the return content and handles it according to each type:

- HTML content is rendered: HTML tags, scripts, CSS, and “noise” are removed from the access result, keeping only the plain text of the link.
- Other textual content: the content is read directly and no transformation is performed.
- Non‐textual content: when the link responds with non‐textual content and the response indicates a filename (either by path or by the `Content‐Disposition` header), the system attempts to convert the downloaded file to a textual version.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "OpenUrl"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Memory

Enable `Remember` when the assistant needs to save information across conversations and retrieve it when relevant. It exposes exactly two tools: `memory_save` and `memory_search`.

Both tools require an identified user: set a stable `tag` in a [chat client](/docs/inference/chat-clients), or `$.user` in a chat/completions request. Without that identifier, the tools return an error. Memory searches are automatically restricted to the current user. Each memory records the gateway that saved it, and `parameters.builtinFunctionsOptions.allowSharedMemory` controls visibility:

| `allowSharedMemory` | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `true` (default) | The gateway reads, replaces, and deletes the user's memories saved by any gateway in the account. |
| `false` | The gateway only reads, replaces, and deletes the user's memories that it saved itself. |

In the dashboard, this is the **Memory visibility** option in the gateway's tool settings. Memories saved outside a saved gateway, and memories migrated from the earlier memory tools, have no gateway and are visible only to gateways with shared memory.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "Remember"
    ]
}
```

Memories are **not automatically added to system instructions**. Tell the model when to call `memory_search`, such as before answering a question about a saved preference. The removed `include_all_memory_context` option, including its `IncludeAllMemoryContext` spelling, is ignored if sent.

### Save, Replace, or Delete a Memory

`memory_save(id?, content?, expiresInDays?)` combines creation, replacement, and deletion. `id` is the memory's ID; `content` is the text to save, limited to 10 KB per saved memory; `expiresInDays` is an optional whole number of days, from 1 to 365, after which the memory is deleted automatically.

| Arguments | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `content`, with `id` omitted or `null` | Creates a memory and returns its ID. Without `expiresInDays`, it never expires. |
| `id` and `content` | Replaces that memory's content. Without `expiresInDays`, the current expiration is kept. |
| `id` and `expiresInDays`, with `content` omitted or `null` | Changes only that memory's expiration, counted from now. |
| Only `id` | Deletes that memory. |
| `id` and `content` both omitted or `null` | Returns an error. |

Only memories belonging to the current user can be replaced or deleted. The former `memory_update`, `memory_remove`, and `memory_clear` tools are no longer available; update instructions and tool-call handling to use `memory_save` for individual changes.

### Search Memories

`memory_search(query?, filter?)` requires **exactly one** argument: `query` or `filter`. Sending both, or neither, returns an error.

| Argument | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `query` | A text query for semantic search over the current user's memories, reranked with `rrf` (Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Returns up to 10 results. |
| `filter` | A string using [AIVAX document filter syntax](/docs/rag/document-filters). Returns up to 10 matching memories, newest first, without generating query embeddings. |

Each result contains `id`, `content`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, and `expiresAt` (`null` when the memory never expires). Expired memories are never returned. Use `query` to find meaning; use `filter` for exact text, metadata, or creation and update dates:

| Goal | `filter` |
| --- | --- |
| Created in the last 7 days | `createdAt >= now-7d` |
| Changed in the last 24 hours | `updatedAt >= now-24h` |
| Created in October 2026 | `createdAt >= "2026-10-01" and createdAt < "2026-11-01"` |
| Not updated for 90 days, for example stale candidates to review | `updatedAt < now-90d` |
| Mentions a birthday and was created in the last 30 days | `content contains "birthday" and createdAt >= now-30d` |
| Saved in a specific conversation | `metadata.conversation_token = "<conversation token>"` |

Dates and timestamps without an offset use the server reference time zone described in [Document filters — Dates](/docs/rag/document-filters#dates). A memory's creation or update date is not the date of an event mentioned in its text.

### Storage and Management

Memories are documents in the `@memories` RAG collection in your AIVAX account. The collection is created automatically on the first save. Each document's content is the memory text, and its metadata identifies the user and originating conversation:

```json
{
    "external_user_id": "<user tag>",
    "conversation_token": "<conversation token>",
    "gateway_id": "<gateway ID>",
    "expires_at": 1791580376
}
```

When no conversation token is available, `conversation_token` is JSON `null`, not a string. `gateway_id` is the ID of the gateway that saved the memory, or `null` when it was not saved by a saved gateway. `expires_at` is a Unix timestamp in seconds, or `null` when the memory never expires. Newly saved or updated memories become searchable after indexing completes, usually within a few seconds.

Memories saved with `expiresInDays` are deleted in a periodic cleanup after they expire; until then they are hidden from `memory_search`. Memories without an expiration are kept until deleted. When managing the collection directly, set or remove `metadata.expires_at` to control expiration. Inspect and manage them in the dashboard's Collections and Documents pages or through the [Collections and Documents APIs](../rag/collections.md). The dedicated Memories API and dashboard Memories page are removed. **Deleting the `@memories` collection erases every user's memories in the account**; the collection is recreated on the next save.

The automatic user restriction applies to the memory tools. When managing the collection directly, use `metadata.external_user_id` to select the intended user's records and preserve the user metadata.

### Billing, Limits, and Errors

Saving or replacing memory content indexes it like any collection document, with document-embedding charges. A `query` search is billed as a RAG query embedding. A `filter` search has no embedding cost, and the `rrf` reranker has no reranking cost. Memory has no separate tool charge; see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits).

Both memory tools use the account's [RAG rate limits](../rag/collections.md#pricing-and-limits). If the account has no balance or reaches a rate limit, the tool returns an error to the model. Instruct the model to report the failure rather than claim it saved or recalled information. For a recent save that is not yet found, allow indexing to finish before searching again.

### Migration from Earlier Memory and Calendar Tools

Existing non-expired memories were moved to each account's `@memories` collection, preserving their original IDs, user identifiers in `external_user_id`, creation dates, and expiration dates in `expires_at`. Migrated records have `conversation_token: null`. They are re-indexed, which is billed as document embedding.

The `Calendar` built-in tool and its appointment tools were removed from the API and dashboard. Existing gateways and Batch workflows have the flag removed automatically, but requests that still include `Calendar` in `builtin_tools.tools` fail: remove it from your requests. Non-expired calendar reminders were migrated to text memories in the form `Reminder at <date> (<n> minutes): <description>`. These are stored text, not scheduled reminders or a replacement calendar service.

The former Memories API, including list, get, delete, and migration prompt generation, is no longer available. Move application-level memory management to the Collections and Documents APIs. Update gateway instructions to search explicitly. Gateways with private memory do not see migrated memories, because migrated records have no `gateway_id`. The former `retentionDays` argument is now `expiresInDays`; omitting it creates a memory that never expires, where the old default was 30 days.

For application-level controls around memory writes, deletion policies, and review, see [How to protect LLM agent memory from poisoning](https://aivax.net/blog/persistent-memory-is-a-write-path/).

## Image Generation

This function allows the model to create AI images.

AI‐generated images are attached to the conversation context, but are not directly visible to the assistant.

Image generation can incur usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling it in production.

You can also enable the generation of explicit and adult images in image generation. When this feature is enabled, the model will be allowed to generate adult material. For this to happen, the model must also “agree” to generate such content. Some models have a lower security filter than others. For example, Gemini models have the lowest security filter, making them a viable option for role‐play and generating such material.

You are always responsible for the [material you generate](/docs/legal/terms-of-service) and the generated material must be compatible with our terms of service.

The available image generation models are listed in the AIVAX console.

Generated images are stored on AIVAX servers for a few months before being permanently removed.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "ImageGeneration"
    ],
    "options": {
        "image_generation_model_name": "grok-imagine",
        "image_generation_allow_reference_usage": true,
        "image_generation_quality": "high",
        "image_generation_max_results": 2,
        "image_generation_allow_mature_content": false
    }
}
```

Model inference used to invoke a tool is still billed at its regular rate. Image generation is billed at the selected model's rates; see [Image generation](../generations/images.md).

| X (Twitter) search | **$5/1k searches** |
| [Memory](#memory) | Saving or replacing content: document embedding; semantic `query` search: RAG query embedding; `filter` search: no embedding cost; `rrf` reranking: no cost |
| Advanced requests | No separate charge |
| Document generation | No separate charge |
| Web page generation | No separate charge |

An em dash (`—`) means the plan does not impose a limit, and `Not available` means the tool is unavailable on the plan.
